ipc-title__text: A very good movie about very bad people
main_review: Throughout history, well-intentioned men have committed many horrible crimes in the name of their mother countries.  THE GODFATHER is about a well-intentioned man named Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) who learns to commit horrible crimes in the name of his family.The Godfather is Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando) who heads one of the most powerful crime families in New York.  He has three sons: hot-tempered Santino (James Caan), weak-willed Fredo (John Cazale), and Michael. "Michael," significantly, is the only Anglicized name of the three.  Michael is the only son who fought for the Americans in World War II, and the only one who wants nothing to do with the family crime business.  He is something of an outsider to his family.But Michael is devoted to his father.  And when Vito is severely wounded in an attempted assassination by drug dealer Virgil "the Turk" Sollozzo, who thinks Vito's heir apparent Santino will be readier to deal with him, then Michael saves his life.  Later, Michael murders the Turk and his hired police bodyguard, knowing that he will have to flee to Sicily for breaking the unwritten truce between the police and the Mafia.The saga of Michael's rise to head the Corleone family is one of the most fascinating stories ever told on screen.  It is hard to tell a good story about evil, but Coppola succeeds, principally because he shows the sincere devotion to family that lies behind the characters' deeds.  Michael is slowly corrupted into a cold-hearted killer, not by laziness or indifference or any other vice, but by his defining virtue: his love for his father and brothers!  Likewise, Santino comes to grief as a direct result of his only redeeming feature, his devotion to his sister.  This tragic irony suffuses the film.  The viewer thus can forgive the characters somewhat for their crimes, because the life they have been born into gives them a choice between violent crime and abandoning their loved ones.Nino Rota's sad, haunting score is superb, and his Siciliana theme is beautiful and tender.  The supporting performances are superb, particularly Abe Vigoda and Richard Castellano as the Godfather's tough but genial caporegimes, Robert Duvall as the "consigliere" or Mafia lawyer, and Al Lettieri as Sollozzo.  Luca Brasi unfortunately disappears too quickly; his role was more fleshed out in Puzo's original novel.Enter a world where murder is "not personal.  It's strictly business."  You will never forget it.Rating: **** out of ****.

This film is pretty much as close to cinematic perfection as you can possibly get. From the very first moments, with its beautiful theme playing on trumpets, it hooks you and doesn't let go for the next three hours. The opening is possibly the best I've ever seen: the first thirty minutes does an incredible job of establishing the setting, characters, and plot points, major and minor, all through dialogue and interactions. From there, it's a roller coaster of exceptional storytelling and character development that's endlessly captivating. And at its heart is the story of one man's rise to power coupled with the start of his fall from grace. Michael starts out as an honest man who wants nothing to do with the family business. But, as their enemies move in on them, he gets roped into that world in the worst way. After seeing the ugliness therein, he makes plans to make the family legitimate, but starts to go too far in his methods of doing so, starting a downward spiral that only gets worse as the series progresses. It's a brilliant character arc that I could probably talk for hours about.It's astonishing to think that Marlon Brando had to fight to be allowed to even be in this movie, because he was truly born for it. He doesn't just play Vito Corleone, he is Vito Corleone, giving him a humble, gentle, yet subtly threatening performance that's easily one of, if not the best, acting job I have ever seen. Al Pacino, a personal favorite, excels as Michael, perfectly showcasing his growth as a character. The later scenes in particular are where he truly shines; all he needs to do is flash that signature glare of his and you know there's trouble waiting. James Caan really should have won the Oscar for his incredible performance. And the rest of the cast is fantastic too. What really makes the performances work, at least in regards of the actors who play the Corleones, is that they truly feel like a genuine family, in more ways than one.From the opening pan out of the old man telling the Don his story to the final shot of Diane Keaton's disturbed look at what her husband's become, Francis Ford Coppola's direction is absolutely incredible. The film is chock full of memorable moments, catchy music, and endlessly quotable dialogue. And it all leads up to a scene that still gives me chills every time I watch this film: the baptism scene. The music, the editing, the buildup and payoff, and the juxtaposition of this sacred ritual against all the horrors being committed at the same time make for a scene that's absolutely flawless and easily a top ten favorite. For the record, I actually got to see this film in theaters a couple of years ago for its fiftieth anniversary, and it was beyond worth the price of admission.Overall, I think I've more than said all I needed to say about The Godfather. Curious if The Godfathers are as good as their 9.2/9.0 ratings on here, I purchased the Bluray-Restoration Trilogy and just now watched the 3-hour first movie...only my second watch, and the first time since 25 years or so.....and my opinion is unchanged! The Godfather is a good film. It's very well made, with tons of neat intelligent scenes and dialogue. Well acted. Fitting music. Decent camera work. But it's also tricky to follow, a few times I wondered who characters were referencing...this isn't a problem I've had with Goodfellas or Sopranos. Michael's relationship drama with his two wives isn't really that compelling, and neither is the paranoid mob war. The motives of the antagonist mobsters don't feel convincing.A couple of action scenes have dated badly. One scene has Sonny punching clear air but the sound effects are claiming contact. Tho' the death scenes were generally done well and still look good today.Curiously, there's often no offered subtitles when the characters talk in Italian. Specifically an important restaurant scene is missing this. I later watched an online clip with the translation, and I disagree with Copolla: the subs should've stayed in. Also, the image-quality isn't that impressive for a claimed 4k-mastering restoration. Very deep blacks for indoor scenes, meaning you struggle to differentiate among all those black suits. I guess they were going for a chiaroscuro-style (like Caravaggio famously employed in his paintings), so this gets a pass.7/10 feels absolutely fair. Yet poll after poll still puts this movie right at the top (or very close) in the all-time rankings.Citizen Kane is one of those I feel deserves such a reputation. The Godfather...not so much.Part II next. Let's see if it holds its 8/10 (hopefully improves on it!).

His gravelly voice and stoic demeanor add layers to the character, making Vito a cinematic legend.Equally impressive is Al Pacino, who plays Vito's youngest son, Michael Corleone. Michael's transformation from a reluctant outsider to a ruthless and calculating mafia boss is the film's emotional and narrative anchor. Pacino's performance is a masterclass in subtlety and restraint, and his ability to convey internal turmoil without overt displays of emotion is mesmerizing.Cinematographer Gordon Willis's work on "The Godfather" is nothing short of revolutionary. Willis's camera work captures the grandeur and intimacy of the Corleone world, while also underscoring the moral ambiguity that permeates every frame.The screenplay, co-written by Coppola and Puzo, is a triumph of adaptation. It is now past 1 PM and I just finished watching Francis Ford Coppola's "The Godfather". I should probably go to bed. It's late and tomorrow I have to wake up a bit early. So, bear with me.This film works so well because it takes place in an underworld in which we are so embedded that we do not even observe it. Coppola puts us straight in the smack-dab center of what is, admittedly, a society made by criminals for criminals. It is also the reason why it's so welcoming. We are surrounded by its inhabitants--cold-blooded murderers, men who see crime like a 9 to 5 job masquerading as honorable men. And I do mean men. From the outside, we would only witness the horrifying, disturbing manifestations of their well-thought out actions.But it goes even deeper than that. It all revolves around the Corleone family led by Don Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando). He is the most honest of these men, sitting right on the edge. But for people like him, who do not fully embrace this world, it's not easy. He avoids conflict until it is absolutely necessary. He is a man defined by moral principles. There is a scene at the beginning, in which, during his daughter's wedding day, one of his associates, Luca Brasi (Lenny Montana) practices his speech that he is going to give to the Don when he meets him. The scene with these two is funny and almost adorable. I could not help but sympathize both of them only to realize that I am feeling warmth for two mobsters. Not to even mention that Lenny Montana was an actual mob hit-man and that he was actually nervous as he said that line.The more I watched the more I realized just how incredibly complex and ruthless this society is and how it has the power to corrupt anyone to come in contact with it. The best example is Corleone's youngest son, Michael (Al Pacino). He returns home for his sister's wedding as a war hero dressed the part with his long-time girlfriend, Kay Adams (Diane Keaton). At first, he avoids this underworld, but necessity, first-hand exposure and just its sheer devilish appealing nature draws him in. As we get further in the film, the change is shocking and every outsider who ever got close to him is tainted in one way or another. If they survive it, they are drawn in as well as we are as viewers.Inside, Coppola exposes the family to us fully, with a bold personal approach and we witness every discussion, every methodically calculated choice. Crime is done simply because it is the nature of their business, and we are put on a chair alongside them, so we easily relate. For us, they are the good guys, the rival families are the bad guys. This is the greatest feat this film managed to pull off--set apart good guys and bad guys in a world filled with bad guys.This is a film of unmatched subtlety. No other movie sustains itself as good. No other film is done with such precision, attention and completeness. There are many layers which I probably missed and maybe will never notice. But I felt them. What director Francis Ford Coppola and his partner in crime (poor choice of words, sorry) Mario Puzo did is nothing short of a timeless piece of reference cinema whose influence is not based on reinventing the wheel, but rather perfecting it to the absolute maximum.Most masterpieces are remembered for their historical contributions. "Citizen Kane" brought the biggest step-up to the art form, the same things did "Gone With the Wind" or "2001: A Space Odyssey". "The Godfather" is one of the few films that will be remembered simply because they are that good and I cannot possibly imagine a greater.

Vito's son, Michael (Al Pacino), wades into the family business and is groomed to eventually lead it.Director Francis Ford Coppola co-wrote the screenplay with Puzo. Pacino also carries the film's mid-section with a series of scenes involving a hospital, a restaurant, and Sicily in that order (a succinct summary). These segments, like others in the film, are intense with perfect build-ups.The film's most powerful scene involves one where Michael is literally being a godfather at his nephew's baptism. The holy atmosphere of the event is contrasted, back and forth, with other scenes (involving family business) that are anything but holy. The polar opposites play brilliantly against each other in an almost sarcastic way.And the film ends with a poignant scene between Michael and his wife, Kay (Diane Keaton), and a powerful closing image. A perfect ending for a perfect film.In addition to the great performances of Pacino, Brando, and Keaton, the excellent cast also includes James Caan, Robert Duvall, Richard Castellano, Sterling Hayden, John Marley, Abe Vigoda, John Cazale, Talia Shire, Gianni Russo, Morgana King, Richard Conte, Lenny Montana and Simonetta Stefanelli."The Godfather" is considered outstanding by film critics as well as movie fans. This is one of those titans of cinema. A film so large and firmly ensconced in the collective consciousness of the film world that one does not speak against it and get taken very seriously. Well, I'm not going to speak against that consensus. Not because I cannot think for myself, but because I see Francis Ford Coppola's work bringing Mario Puzo's kinda trashy mobster novel to film and find a film of such craft and care in its construction at every level, all in service towards a central tragedy, that I cannot deny the immense achievement that The Godfather is. It's something of a fulcrum film, vacillating between the precise classical construction that Hollywood had steadily built over decades with the more explicit treatments of sex and violence.I think one of the reasons this film works so well is that it works both as a family saga and an intimate character portrait, and that they intertwine, interrelate, and inform each other. The saga is of course around the potential fall of the Corleone crime family in New York. Headed by Don Vito (Marlon Brando), the Corleone's are a well-respected family both inside and outside the underworld of the mob. He's spent decades building up contacts around New York, and all of this gets introduced in the bravura opening half hour of the film. It would surprise me if this didn't influence Ingmar Bergman when he made Fanny and Alexander, but the introductory wedding is an amazing piece of filmmaking that bounces from family business, to the business of the wedding, and back, all while introducing at least two dozen characters, all of whom will have their parts to play in the coming drama. The center of it all is the late attendee Michael (Al Pacino), the youngest son of Don Vito, fresh from service in WWII with his girl Kay (Diane Keaton) on his arm. It is through his interactions with her that we get our explicit tellings, like how he explains how Vito got the Frank Sinatra stand-in, Johnny Fontane (Al Martino), out of his limiting contract years ago, by Vito putting a gun to his contract holder's head and saying that either the signature or the brains will be on it. The offer he couldn't refuse. It's also important that Michael says that the story reflects his family but not himself.Michael is the civilian of the family while everyone else, in particular his two older brothers Sonny (James Caan) and Fredo (John Cazale), are active members of the business. Vito seems to want something different for Michael, which is why he went to college instead of into the business. The irony is that had Sollozzo (Al Lettieri) accepted Vito's answer of no of entering the drug business (he couldn't because Vito had too much singular political control), then Sollozzo might have ended up in a better place. The idea was that Sonny wanted the deal to get into the drug trade, so if Vito is put out of the way, Sonny takes control of the family, and, after a cooling off period from the murder of his father, he'd relinquish control, or enter into a war that he'd fight poorly and lose. If not for Michael, that could have happened, but Michael was simply too cool-headed, to careful, and too vicious to let Sollozzo and his hidden allies in the other five families of New York get away with it.My father loves this film, and when we'd watch it together when I was young, he liked to point out a specific moment when Michael crosses his legs as the moment he becomes the "godfather", the head of the family. It's in the background of a tracking shot following Sonny, and he has a point. However, there's a moment earlier, when Michael goes to the hospital to visit his father, recovering from Sollozzo's assassination attempt, where Michael takes charge like no one else in the family could, shuffling around a few pieces to create an impression of strength that carries over to the outside world. Is that when he becomes head of the family? No, but it is when he enters the business and shows that he's more capable and smarter than anyone else, and that is a tragedy. It's born of love for his father, to see him simply not murdered, but Michael's intelligence ends up getting put into the service of a crime family where he directs murder.The most curious part of the film is the central section after Michael kills Sollozzo and the police captain McCluskey (Sterling Hayden) and he retreats to Sicily, a place he'd never lived to survive in hiding under the protection of a local don. It's here where Michael tries to lead a normal life. Having left behind Kay and sacrificed his own life for his family, he tries to settle down with the local girl Apollonia (Simonetta Steganelli), marrying her only to watch her die in an assassination attempt for him. His efforts to help his family have marked him for life, and there's only so running he can do.The final hour or so of the film is the tragedy unfolding. It's Vito handing control of the family to Michael, the only competent son he has left. It's Michael looking to the future for the family, talking about respectability, but also investing in the drug trade while doing everything behind the scenes to figure out who had backed Sollozzo, who from his own family might have helped, and organizing a move out of the area to start afresh by going west. It's here where Michael's full potential comes forth, and it's terrifying. His cool viciousness comes out, especially in his interactions with Kay. His lies are so easy and backing such a terrible truth while he completely cements his position as the head of a crime family that it's ultimately tragic to see this young man, this veteran of the Second World War, whom his father talked about becoming Senator Corleone, just following in his father's footsteps to become, perhaps, something worse than his father.As I wrote earlier, the real triumph of this film is the combination of the small scale story of Michael's journey with the larger saga that plays out over a decade from 1945 to 1955 (seriously, years pass between scenes). It's a really intelligent interweaving of interrelated stories as Michael's personal journey influences the saga, giving it deeper meaning, while it goes the other way as well. This approach to the combination of intimate and scale is hardly ever this good in film because it requires a really talented mind to bring it about, and Francis Ford Coppola, result of the Roger Corman system, was that person. The production of Apocalypse Now might have broken his brain, but that was still a few years in the future. This was Coppola making himself known at a scale and with results that make his talent undeniable.The story is tragic. The craft is impeccable. The acting is perfect. This is a titan of American cinema for a reason.

main_review: "The Godfather" stands as a cinematic masterpiece and a monumental achievement in the crime drama genre. Adapted from Mario Puzo's best-selling novel of the same name, the film delves into the world of the Corleone crime family, their struggles for power, and the complexities of loyalty and family ties.At its core, "The Godfather" is a tale of power, ambition, and the consequences that come with living a life within the underworld. The narrative revolves around Don Vito Corleone, portrayed with haunting intensity by Marlon Brando. Brando's performance is nothing short of mesmerizing, with his iconic raspy voice and commanding presence, making him one of the most memorable characters in cinematic history. He portrays Vito as a man of principles, who operates by his own moral code in the world of crime.The film's central focus is on Vito's son, Michael Corleone, played brilliantly by Al Pacino. Michael starts as an outsider, choosing to distance himself from the family business and opting for a more legitimate path. However, as circumstances force him to take on a more active role, we witness his gradual transformation into a ruthless and calculating leader. Pacino's portrayal of Michael's character arc is nothing short of astonishing, showcasing his talent and range as an actor.The supporting cast also delivers outstanding performances, contributing to the film's overall brilliance. James Caan as hotheaded Sonny Corleone, Robert Duvall as the loyal family consigliere Tom Hagen, and Diane Keaton as Michael's love interest Kay Adams, all provide memorable and compelling performances that add depth to the narrative.One of the film's greatest strengths lies in Coppola's masterful direction and attention to detail. The pacing is deliberate, allowing the story to unfold naturally while building suspense and tension. Coppola's use of shadow and light in cinematography gives the film an atmospheric and visually striking quality. The iconic score composed by Nino Rota further elevates the emotional impact of pivotal scenes, leaving an indelible mark on the viewer's memory.Moreover, "The Godfather" boasts a rich and well-developed script that seamlessly blends powerful dialogues with intense and emotionally charged moments. The film skillfully explores themes of loyalty, tradition, family dynamics, and the price of power. It humanizes the characters, making them relatable despite their morally questionable actions.In addition to its compelling storytelling, "The Godfather" is a testament to meticulous set design and authentic period detail. The movie effortlessly transports viewers back to the 1940s and immerses them in the world of the mafia, thanks to the attention given to costumes, props, and locations."The Godfather" had an immense impact on the film industry, shaping the crime drama genre and inspiring numerous subsequent films. It earned eleven Academy Award nominations, with Brando winning the Best Actor award for his iconic performance. The film also secured Oscars for Best Picture and Best Adapted Screenplay, highlighting its enduring legacy and influence.Even after five decades, "The Godfather" continues to be revered and celebrated by critics and audiences alike. It remains a benchmark of cinematic excellence, and its cultural impact is still felt today. From its unforgettable dialogues to its profound exploration of human nature, the film stands as a timeless work of art.In conclusion, "The Godfather" (1972) is a cinematic triumph that remains unrivaled in its genre. Francis Ford Coppola's direction, the outstanding performances of its cast, and the engrossing storytelling combine to create a captivating and unforgettable cinematic experience. This timeless classic will continue to captivate generations to come, solidifying its place as one of the greatest films in cinema history.

You've probably heard again and again how either this is the greatest movie ever made, or that only Citizen Kane tops it. I'm in the latter category.To be honest, I watched it for the 4th time recently, and that's when it made my Top 10. My first time was when I was 18- I'm 24 now. It was the first movie I saw as an adult.I thought it was good, don't get me wrong, but I didn't fully understand why it was so highly regarded. A few months pass, and I watch it on TV. I liked it more. When I was 19, I saw it again on DVD, and I liked it even more.5 years have now passed, and I finally appreciated it the way I, a film buff, should have. And there it went, in the Top 10 best movies I have ever seen.The Godfather is set in Post-WWII New York, and focuses on the Corleone family. They're in The Mafia (a word never spoken in the film, the real Mafia requested this), and if someone betrays the family, they are hunted down and murdered.The Don, Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando), is getting old and his health is deteriorating, and he asks his godson Michael (Al Pacino) to take over the family business. Michael is reluctant, but he eventually agrees to uphold his family's honor.The Godfather is so iconic that any praise I'd give it is nearly pointless. I can add very little to what others already have. Among the most iconic is the famous scenes and lines.From the opening request of murder to avenge for the murder of a daughter, to the subsequent wedding scene, from the horse head in bed (which was real, by the way) to the baptism scene, so many segments have been ingrained into our modern culture.The same goes for many lines. That is the closest I can come to faulting The Godfather, an otherwise exquisite masterpiece. And that's extremely minor.The Godfather is without a doubt one of the greatest contributions to cinema. Regardless of if you are a film buff or a casual viewer, it is a must see. You may be like me and need to grow and see it more than once but trust me when I say that it is the grand film that it is regarded as.

It is now past 1 PM and I just finished watching Francis Ford Coppola's "The Godfather". I should probably go to bed. It's late and tomorrow I have to wake up a bit early. But not early enough to postpone writing these lines. Now that I have seen it three times, the opportunity of sharing my thoughts and refreshed insights are too much of a good offer to sit on. So, bear with me.This film works so well because it takes place in an underworld in which we are so embedded that we do not even observe it. Coppola puts us straight in the smack-dab center of what is, admittedly, a society made by criminals for criminals. It is also the reason why it's so welcoming. We are surrounded by its inhabitants--cold-blooded murderers, men who see crime like a 9 to 5 job masquerading as honorable men. And I do mean men. From the outside, we would only witness the horrifying, disturbing manifestations of their well-thought out actions.But it goes even deeper than that. It all revolves around the Corleone family led by Don Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando). He is the most honest of these men, sitting right on the edge. But for people like him, who do not fully embrace this world, it's not easy. He avoids conflict until it is absolutely necessary. He is a man defined by moral principles. There is a scene at the beginning, in which, during his daughter's wedding day, one of his associates, Luca Brasi (Lenny Montana) practices his speech that he is going to give to the Don when he meets him. The scene with these two is funny and almost adorable. I could not help but sympathize both of them only to realize that I am feeling warmth for two mobsters. Not to even mention that Lenny Montana was an actual mob hit-man and that he was actually nervous as he said that line.The more I watched the more I realized just how incredibly complex and ruthless this society is and how it has the power to corrupt anyone to come in contact with it. The best example is Corleone's youngest son, Michael (Al Pacino). He returns home for his sister's wedding as a war hero dressed the part with his long-time girlfriend, Kay Adams (Diane Keaton). At first, he avoids this underworld, but necessity, first-hand exposure and just its sheer devilish appealing nature draws him in. As we get further in the film, the change is shocking and every outsider who ever got close to him is tainted in one way or another. If they survive it, they are drawn in as well as we are as viewers.Inside, Coppola exposes the family to us fully, with a bold personal approach and we witness every discussion, every methodically calculated choice. Crime is done simply because it is the nature of their business, and we are put on a chair alongside them, so we easily relate. For us, they are the good guys, the rival families are the bad guys. This is the greatest feat this film managed to pull off--set apart good guys and bad guys in a world filled with bad guys.This is a film of unmatched subtlety. No other movie sustains itself as good. No other film is done with such precision, attention and completeness. There are many layers which I probably missed and maybe will never notice. But I felt them. What director Francis Ford Coppola and his partner in crime (poor choice of words, sorry) Mario Puzo did is nothing short of a timeless piece of reference cinema whose influence is not based on reinventing the wheel, but rather perfecting it to the absolute maximum.

This is a masterpiece. A timeless masterpiece. Initially, I didn't like this film all that much - I found it rather over-hyped and boring. This was until the advent of DVD, which gave me the feature I needed for this sort of film: subtitles. Once I switched them on and heard (read) every last word of Brando's ramblings and other characters ramblings, I grew a true appreciation for this epic.To make a true epic, you need all of three following ingredients working in near perfect harmony. For screenwriters who come across this, take the following pointers on board: 1) Contrasting Characters: Good films have some character distinction, but most fall rather flat because the core of each character is the same.Of course, there are exceptions to rule (ie... where you want mono-tonal characters... aka matrix; or where you want outlandish contrasts... aka The Fifth Element), but ultimately, this is what makes films deep, meaningful and grand. Consider the contrasts between the Don's children. Michael is rather cool, rational and collected, whereas Sonny is more hot-headed, spontaneous and simple minded. But simply having these contrasts is not nearly enough. What you really need to do is to develop these characters - place them in situations - and then dwell on how their character impacts on the situation they're put in. The Godfather is a terrific example of how to pull this off. While many try to do this in screenplays, most lose the plot and create character obscurities that stretch credibility.2) Transformation: The central character(s) must undergo a transformation, resulting in them being almost unrecognizable by the end of the film. By putting them into situations, the character's character must not only influence the outcome of the situation; it must also have a lasting impact on the character. Consider Michael at the wedding and compare that to the Michael we see at the end of the film. Again, many films try, but most fail because they come up with unreal (literally, not praisingly) or simply moronic transformations (eg, Wall Street).3) Patience: Men in Black 2 was an astounding film for one simple reason - it was an entire film squashed into about 70 minutes. It was not much longer than an episode of ER or Buffy. I certainly hope the new goal of Hollywood isn't to make films as short as possible.All the great ones spend time - time developing characters, family life, growth, patience with the story telling in general. This is the key (provided that the story isn't mind-numbingly boring). Dances with Wolves, Heat.. and so on are very patient but top-class films. While studios may be lukewarm on the idea of longer films, they are worth it if you have a ripper story to base it on.I feel that this film has not dated all that much and has tremendous re-watch-ability.

main_review: I was roughly twenty years away from even being conceived when The Godfather came out. Growing up as a film nut, I often heard of The Godfather as possessing a sort of mythic status that few films made after 1955 possess. I first watched it back close to ten years ago as a 12-year-old, never fully getting the story with the film falling into the "great film that I didn't appreciate" category until a month or so back when I got the Coppola restoration Blu-Ray and realized as an adult how fantastic of a film it truly was. The Godfather works so well because it isn't a film that kisses its ass on a variety of sub-levels. Francis Ford Coppola went out of his way not to make the film one that glorifies the Mafia in any way but still realized what a magnificent project it was. It begins in celebration and ends as the first part of the trilogy in bitter-sweet victory and tragedy for the Corleones with Michael having slowly morphed into a different character by the end and the Corleone family itself has endured tragedy after tragedy. Depending on if you're selective to certain genres of movies -- particularly crime and heist thrillers -- the 1970s were either a fantastic time with the New Hollywood group of directors or a pitiful time where the Anti-Hero was all the rage. I've always tried to keep a foot in both camps for the most part, but if a film like this doesn't make you at least sit there as the credits roll, musing in thought like Indiana Jones after being given a clue by a recently-killed shaman or anti-Nazi spy the first time you watch it, then I'm not sure you know how to appreciate films and movies as art and not just entertainment. There are so many ways this film just works so well; the first is that Coppola always had a way of making the cinematography and direction style look both extravagant, but also bleak at the same time, partially through sun-faded cinematography (I'm just guessing) and also partially through the way the film itself was shot. As well fact that Coppola spared nothing when it came to deploying talented screen stars of the day to cast The Godfather, leading Marlon Brando to find international success once more with his portrayal of Vito Corleone, Al Pacino as the reluctant, but the eventual successor to his father Vito, Michael Corleone, Diane Keaton as Kay Adams, Robert Duvall as Tom Hagen, and of course, a pre-Rocky Talia Shire as Connie Corleone. These cast members in particular stand out in their performances and convey a sort of detached emotion that makes the film so great (if you need clarification on this, the scene where Vito overlooks his own son's body in the morgue is a prime example). Although it is the best install installment Godfather trilogy, the film itself suffers from a few key points that I've never been able to reason out why were included. Specifically, the whole sequence involves Johnny Fontaine and the Woltz horse fiasco which has no real involvement in the over-arcing storyline. However, with how spectacular of a film it is, I'm not going to sit here and complain about it any further.
